clue.text: Thesaurus explanation gaining currency

parts.note: a thesaurus is literally a treasury or storehouse of words
a note is a brief explanation or annotation

explanation.surface: A reference book of synonyms adds an explanatory gloss and becomes widely accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Currency' looks like popularity of a word, but it means money: a TREASURY NOTE was paper money issued by the UK Treasury.
explanation.definitionFit: A Treasury note was a banknote issued by the British Treasury, so it is a form of money.

clue.text: Action painting of match is poor

indicators.note: poor suggests something badly made, so the letters of match and is are put together in a new, worse order

explanation.surface: Painting done in an energetic style ruins a game of football, apparently.
explanation.definitionFit: Tachism is a French abstract style in which paint is splashed or dabbed, also called action painting.

clue.text: Cockney handles mischievous children

indicators.note: Cockney speech drops the initial aitch, so the H goes from the front of the word

parts.note: helves are the handles of axes or hammers

explanation.surface: A London East Ender grabs some naughty kids.
explanation.walkthrough: Cockney is the working-class dialect of East London, famous for dropping the H sound at the start of words.
explanation.definitionFit: Elves are mischievous sprites, a playful term for naughty little children.

clue.text: The battlefield is bright crimson

explanation.surface: A field of war is described as vividly red, as if with blood.
explanation.definitionFit: Solferino is the 1859 battle in Lombardy, and a vivid purplish-red aniline dye was named after it.

clue.text: Horse running under two colours

parts.note: reads like a racehorse in its owner's racing silks, but means a horse whose coat mixes two colours, as of reddish brown or black flecked with white

explanation.surface: A racehorse runs in an owner's two-colour silks.
explanation.definitionFit: A roan horse has a coat in which white hairs are mixed through a darker base colour.

clue.text: Send eels off — not wanted here

indicators.note: off suggests something gone bad or out of order, so the letters of send eels are rearranged

explanation.surface: A fishmonger told to send the eels away, as nobody wants them here.
explanation.definitionFit: Something needless is unnecessary, not wanted or required.

clue.text: Sum me up as the image of my family, perhaps

parts.note: a tot is a sum of figures added up, as in tot up

indicators.note: in a down clue up means the word me is read from bottom to top, backwards

explanation.surface: Someone asks to be summed up as a symbol of their own clan.
explanation.definitionFit: A totem is an emblem, often an animal or carved figure, representing a family or clan.

clue.text: Need girl be made to put a belt on?

indicators.note: being made into something else implies the letters of need girl are reworked into a new word

explanation.surface: Does a girl in need have to be forced to wear a belt?
explanation.definitionFit: To engirdle is to encircle or surround with a girdle, that is, to belt.

clue.text: Scottish critic familiar with Fletcher's works

explanation.surface: A Scottish reviewer knows the plays of the Jacobean dramatist John Fletcher well.
explanation.walkthrough: John Fletcher the playwright is a red herring: a fletcher is a maker of arrows, whose works an archer handles. William Archer was a Scottish drama critic.
explanation.definitionFit: William Archer was a Scottish theatre critic; a bowman uses the arrows a fletcher makes.

clue.text: Cowardly show, motorists in train!

explanation.surface: A timid display: drivers travelling by rail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cowardly' looks like timid, but means by Noel Coward, whose play Cavalcade was staged in 1931.
explanation.definitionFit: Cavalcade is a Noel Coward play; a procession of vehicles following one another in line is also so called.

clue.text: 'A professional note-writer for the speaker

parts.note: reads as a speechwriter, but points to someone whose trade is getting musical notes right, as with a piano, and to the radio unit that feeds a loudspeaker

explanation.surface: A hired hand drafts notes for someone giving a speech.
explanation.definitionFit: A piano tuner adjusts the pitch of notes professionally, and a hi-fi tuner supplies the signal to the speakers.

clue.text: Popular favourites backed together

parts.note: in means fashionable or popular

indicators.note: backed means the word for favourites is read backwards

parts.note: pets are favourites, as in teacher's pet

explanation.surface: Well-liked favourites support each other.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in step means moving in unison, in agreement with others.

clue.text: It's a mistake to admit tired reactionary

indicators.note: to admit is to let in, so one word goes inside the other

parts.note: bish is British slang for a blunder or mistake
limp means drooping or tired

explanation.surface: Someone admits that their weary, backward-looking views are an error.
explanation.walkthrough: Colonel Blimp was a cartoon character of pompous British reactionary views.
explanation.definitionFit: Blimpish describes the pompous, diehard conservatism of the cartoon figure Colonel Blimp.

clue.text: Bird familiar in shooting circles

explanation.surface: A common bird is well known among people who shoot.
explanation.walkthrough: On a rifle target, a magpie is a shot striking the ring next to the outermost one.
explanation.definitionFit: The magpie is a well-known black-and-white corvid, and in target shooting it names a hit in the second-outermost ring.

clue.text: Speaks to the point, she does

indicators.note: speaks means the word is said out loud and the spelling of the woman's name follows its sound

parts.note: germane means relevant, to the point

explanation.surface: She speaks only when relevant, so she does.
explanation.definitionFit: Germaine is a woman's given name, as with the writer Germaine Greer.

clue.text: One gets false report listening to white man perhaps

parts.note: one is I, the Roman numeral
slander is a false and damaging spoken report

explanation.surface: Someone is told lies while hearing out a white man.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition says 'white man' heard aloud, giving Wight man: a man of the Isle of Wight, off England's south coast; the Isle of Man also hides in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A man from the Isle of Wight, or of Man, lives on an island, so is an island dweller.

clue.text: Duke of York's contradictory hilltop order?

definitions.text: Duke of York's contradictory hilltop order?

parts.words: Duke of York's contradictory hilltop order
parts.note: the nursery rhyme Grand Old Duke of York marches ten thousand men up a hill and down again, so at the top he must command them to reverse direction

explanation.surface: A nursery-rhyme duke gives a confusing command at the top of a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: The Grand Old Duke of York is an English nursery rhyme in which troops march up a hill and straight back down.
explanation.definitionFit: A military command to turn and face the opposite way is what marching back down a hill requires.

clue.text: Delightful drawing

explanation.surface: Someone praises a charming sketch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' looks like a picture, but here means drawing water, going to get it.
explanation.definitionFit: Fetching means attractive or charming; it also means going for and bringing back, as drawing water.

clue.text: Cleric whose indulgence one might seek

definitions.text: Cleric whose indulgence one might seek

parts.words: Cleric whose indulgence one might seek
parts.note: a medieval churchman who sold papal indulgences, as in Chaucer, with forgiveness being what the sinner asks for

explanation.surface: A churchman whose leniency a sinner hopes to win.
explanation.walkthrough: Indulgences were remissions of punishment for sin sold by the medieval church; Chaucer's Canterbury Tales has one such seller.
explanation.definitionFit: A pardoner was a medieval cleric licensed to sell papal indulgences, remissions of sin.

clue.text: French scientist, discoverer of sulphur in different states

indicators.note: in means the sulphur symbol goes inside the pair of state abbreviations

parts.note: PA is Pennsylvania
CAL is California, a second US state
S is the chemical symbol for sulphur

explanation.surface: A French chemist found sulphur in several different forms.
explanation.walkthrough: 'States' looks like physical states of matter; it means two US states.
explanation.definitionFit: Blaise Pascal was a French mathematician and physicist who discovered the principle of fluid pressure.

clue.text: Fellow going back years in the wine cellar

parts.note: bod is British slang for a person or fellow

indicators.note: going back means the word for years is read in reverse

parts.note: an age is a long span of years

explanation.surface: An old chap has spent years down in the wine cellar.
explanation.definitionFit: A bodega is a Spanish cellar or shop for storing and selling wine.

clue.text: Sailor assaulted, we hear, and injured

indicators.note: we hear means the words are taken as spoken and the entry follows their sound

parts.note: AB is an able seaman, a sailor, and raided means assaulted

explanation.surface: A sailor was attacked, we are told, and hurt.
explanation.definitionFit: Abraded means scraped or worn away, as skin in a graze, so hurt.

clue.text: Had crash, somehow emerged unharmed from fire

definitions.note: a verb phrase standing for the man who did so

indicators.note: somehow suggests things put together in some unknown way, so the letters of had crash are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone crashed and somehow walked out of the burning wreck unhurt.
explanation.walkthrough: In the Book of Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego were thrown into a fiery furnace and came out unharmed.
explanation.definitionFit: Shadrach is the biblical young man who survived Nebuchadnezzar's fiery furnace.

clue.text: Doorkeeper upset, being fired again

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the word is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: a tyler or tiler is the doorkeeper of a Masonic lodge

explanation.surface: A porter is upset at being sacked a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fired' looks like sacked, but means set alight.
explanation.definitionFit: Relit means set alight once more, as a fire or pipe.

clue.text: Such a cheque must distress 16.

indicators.note: to distress is to batter or disturb, so the letters of must are jumbled

parts.note: the cross-reference sends the solver to 16-down's two words read as an instruction: RE (about) and then turned around

explanation.surface: A bounced cheque is bound to upset the person named at 16.
explanation.walkthrough: The '16' is used as wordplay: its two words read as 'about' (RE) and 'turn', which reverses it to ER. Stumer is old British slang.
explanation.definitionFit: A stumer is slang for a dud or worthless cheque, one that bounces.

clue.text: Motherly follower of a heathen prince?

definitions.text: Motherly follower of a heathen prince?

parts.note: ma is a familiar word for mother
Gog is the heathen prince of ... in the Book of Ezekiel

explanation.surface: Someone asks whether a mother figure follows a pagan ruler.
explanation.walkthrough: Gog and Magog appear together in the Bible and in London legend, so the second always follows the first.
explanation.definitionFit: Magog is paired with and follows Gog, the biblical heathen ruler, as in Gog and Magog.

clue.text: Lean diet

explanation.surface: Someone thin is on a weight-loss plan.
explanation.definitionFit: Slim means thin as an adjective, and to slim is to reduce weight by dieting.

clue.text: One of Gray's poor records — short and simple

definitions.text: One of Gray's poor records — short and simple

parts.words: One of Gray's poor records — short and simple
parts.note: quotes Thomas Gray's Elegy in a Country Churchyard, which speaks of the short and simple yearly chronicles of the poor

explanation.surface: A poet's records of humble folk are brief and plain.
explanation.walkthrough: Gray's Elegy line runs 'The short and simple annals of the poor'; 'poor' looks like low-quality but means poor people.
explanation.definitionFit: An annal is a single year's entry in a historical chronicle.

clue.text: Rash wrongly suspected

explanation.surface: A skin complaint has been misdiagnosed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rash' looks like a skin complaint but means reckless.
explanation.definitionFit: Ill-judged means unwise or reckless; it also describes someone misjudged, assessed wrongly.

clue.text: The drama ran, being effectively presented

parts.note: the stage stands for the theatre or drama as a whole
to run a business is to manage it

explanation.surface: The play ran on, presented to good effect.
explanation.definitionFit: Stage-managed means skilfully arranged for effect, controlled behind the scenes.
